messages.content: I want to enable zero-shot voice conversion across unseen tonal languages while transferring speaker identity without altering lexical tone or prosody. How should I state the goal precisely?

The goal is to make a voice sound like a target speaker even when the tonal language is unseen, while retaining what the source speech expresses through lexical tone, intonation, and rhythm. “Zero-shot” and “unseen tonal languages” describe the intended setting; they do not, by themselves, specify a method or establish that the goal has been achieved.
Does transferring speaker identity mean the converted speech should also adopt the target speaker’s intonation?

Not under this goal. Speaker identity is what should transfer from the target speaker. The source speech’s lexical tone, intonation, and rhythm should remain intact. That distinction matters because sounding like the target speaker is not sufficient if the conversion changes tonal meaning or reshapes the source prosody.
What makes lexical tone a separate concern from prosody here?

Lexical tone is specifically called out because altering it can change the tonal distinctions carried by the source speech. The goal also explicitly protects source intonation and rhythm. These requirements belong together, but the lexical-tone requirement has its own numerical error criterion, whereas preservation of intonation and rhythm is stated without a separate numerical threshold.
What exactly is the numerical criterion for lexical tone?

Lexical-tone error in converted speech should be within 2 percentage points of lexical-tone error in unconverted speech. The unconverted speech is the comparison baseline. This is a difference measured in percentage points, not a requirement that lexical-tone error itself be 2%, and not a relative change of 2%.
So the comparison is against the original speech, not against a fixed universal error rate?

Yes. The stated comparison is with unconverted speech. It asks that conversion leave lexical-tone error close to that baseline—within 2 percentage points—while preserving the source intonation and rhythm. It does not supply an absolute lexical-tone error rate for every language or utterance.
When I say “within 2 percentage points,” should I avoid calling that “2 percent better” or “2 percent worse”?

Yes. “Percentage points” refers to the difference between two error rates expressed as percentages. Calling it a 2% relative improvement or deterioration would describe a different calculation. The safest wording is simply that converted-speech lexical-tone error must remain within 2 percentage points of the unconverted-speech error.
And the source intonation and rhythm are part of the same preservation requirement?

They are. The goal is not merely to retain recognizable tonal categories while allowing the rest of the delivery to change. It calls for preserving source intonation and rhythm as well, even as the perceived speaker identity changes.
Can I describe this as changing who seems to be speaking without changing how the source utterance is delivered?

That conveys the central distinction, provided “how it is delivered” is understood here to include the source lexical tone, intonation, and rhythm. It should not be taken to mean that no audible aspect of the voice changes: transferring speaker identity is itself the intended audible change.
What is the separate success criterion for the target speaker’s identity?

The requirement is 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at a 1% false-acceptance rate. In other words, at the specified false-acceptance operating point, the converted speech should be accepted as the target speaker 90% of the time under the stated evaluation criterion.
Is the 1% figure the allowed error in lexical tone?

No. The 1% false-acceptance rate belongs to target-speaker verification. The lexical-tone comparison is the separate requirement that error remain within 2 percentage points of unconverted speech. Those figures measure different aspects of the goal and should not be combined.
Why include the false-acceptance rate when stating the 90% speaker-acceptance target?

It fixes the verification operating point for that target. Saying only “90% acceptance” would omit the stated condition under which acceptance is assessed. The full requirement is 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at 1% false acceptance.
Does that verification result need to come from the same system used during training?

No. The requirement explicitly calls for evaluators independent of training. The speaker-verification target should therefore be assessed with evaluators independent of training, rather than treated as established by a training-time measure alone. The goal does not specify a particular evaluator or evaluation procedure beyond that independence condition.
Could strong speaker verification alone count as success?

No. It addresses whether the target-speaker identity transfers, but the goal also requires zero-shot operation across unseen tonal languages and preservation of the source speech’s lexical tone and prosody. Meeting the speaker-verification target would not, by itself, establish that lexical-tone error stays within 2 percentage points of unconverted speech or that source intonation and rhythm are preserved.
Conversely, if lexical tone, intonation, and rhythm are preserved, is that enough?

Not by itself. Those properties protect what the source speech conveys and how it unfolds, but the voice must also transfer the target speaker’s identity. The stated quantitative identity criterion is 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at 1% false acceptance, using evaluators independent of training.
How much does “across unseen tonal languages” commit me to saying about particular languages?

It identifies the intended scope without naming any languages. The goal concerns zero-shot conversion when the tonal languages are unseen; it does not list languages, define a test set, or give language-by-language results. Those details should not be implied.
Should I say that a particular architecture or adaptation procedure is needed to reach this?

No method is specified in the goal. You can describe the desired behavior and its evaluation criteria, but naming an architecture, a training recipe, or an adaptation procedure would add a decision that has not been stated.
Does “zero-shot” mean the target-speaker acceptance threshold is relaxed for unseen languages?

No relaxation is stated. Zero-shot conversion across unseen tonal languages is part of the goal, and the stated requirements remain lexical-tone error within 2 percentage points of unconverted speech, preservation of source intonation and rhythm, and 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at 1% false acceptance using evaluators independent of training.
I want to make clear that these numbers are targets rather than reported outcomes. How would you phrase that?

Use prospective wording: “The system should keep lexical-tone error within 2 percentage points of unconverted speech” and “It should achieve 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at 1% false acceptance, using evaluators independent of training.” That states the requirements without claiming they have already been measured or met.
Can you put the whole objective in one concise paragraph without losing the distinction between the two measurements?

Enable zero-shot voice conversion across unseen tonal languages that transfers target-speaker identity without altering the source speech’s lexical tone or prosody. Keep lexical-tone error within 2 percentage points of unconverted speech while preserving source intonation and rhythm. Achieve 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at a 1% false-acceptance rate, as measured by evaluators independent of training.
One last distinction: is “preserve prosody” meant to replace the explicit references to intonation and rhythm?

No. “Prosody” expresses the broad aim, while the requirement explicitly names source intonation and rhythm. Keeping those terms visible makes clear what is to remain with the source speech as speaker identity is transferred.
What approach could we propose for the zero-shot voice-conversion goal?

One proposal is to condition a zero-shot flow vocoder on XLS-R content, source F0, source energy, and source durations, together with pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings. The intended separation is that the source supplies the content and prosodic information to retain, while the target-speaker embeddings supply the identity to transfer. This is a proposed configuration, not an established result.
Can you spell out which information comes from the source and which comes from the target?

The XLS-R content representation and the F0, energy, and durations are conditioned on the source speech. The speaker embeddings represent the target speaker and are pitch-adversarial. All of these condition the zero-shot flow vocoder; the proposal does not say to replace the source F0 or timing with the target speaker’s.
Why specify F0 separately if the model already receives XLS-R content?

They have different stated roles in the proposal. XLS-R content provides content conditioning, while source F0 explicitly supplies pitch information from the utterance being converted. For tonal speech, retaining that source-side pitch information is relevant to the aim of not altering lexical tone. The proposal does not claim that either input, alone or in combination, has already met the lexical-tone requirement.
Does source F0 stand in for all of the source prosody?

No. F0 is the pitch-related conditioning input, but the proposal also names source energy and durations. Keeping those inputs distinct makes clear that the vocoder is conditioned on more than a pitch contour: it also receives source-side energy and timing information.
What are durations doing in that list?

Durations provide source-side timing information. Their inclusion is consistent with the goal of retaining the source rhythm rather than treating target-speaker identity as a reason to change when parts of the utterance occur. The node does not specify how durations are obtained or represented.
And how should I talk about energy without claiming too much?

You can say that source energy is another conditioning signal carrying information about the source utterance’s delivery. It belongs alongside source F0 and durations in the proposed conditioning. You need not claim that energy alone preserves intonation or rhythm, or specify a particular energy measurement, because neither is stated.
What does it mean for the target-speaker embeddings to be pitch-adversarial?

It characterizes the proposed target-speaker embeddings: they are intended to represent speaker identity while discouraging pitch information from being encoded as part of that identity representation. That fits the desired division of labor, where source F0 remains available as its own input. The proposal does not specify the adversarial mechanism or demonstrate that the embeddings contain no pitch information.
Is the point to make the target speaker’s pitch disappear from the output?

That would be too strong. The proposal separates source F0 conditioning from pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings so that transferring identity need not entail replacing the source pitch pattern. It does not assert that the converted voice will have no pitch characteristics associated with the target speaker, or that the source contour will be perfectly preserved.
So should I describe the embeddings as the sole source of speaker identity?

The proposal explicitly uses target-speaker embeddings to condition the vocoder for identity transfer. Calling them the sole possible source of every speaker-related cue would go beyond what is stated. The important distinction here is that the embeddings are target-speaker inputs, whereas XLS-R content, F0, energy, and durations are source-side inputs.
Why call it a flow vocoder rather than just a voice-conversion model?

Because the proposed component is specifically a zero-shot flow vocoder, and the proposal specifies what conditions it receives. “Voice-conversion model” would be a broader description, but it would omit the flow-vocoder choice. The node does not give a more detailed flow architecture.
Does zero-shot here commit us to a particular way of obtaining a target-speaker embedding?

No. Zero-shot describes the intended conversion setting, and target-speaker embeddings are part of the proposed conditioning. The proposal does not specify how those embeddings are extracted, what target-speaker material is available, or whether any particular enrollment procedure is used.
Could I say that XLS-R has already been shown to preserve lexical tone across the unseen languages?

Not on the basis of this proposal. It names XLS-R content as a conditioning input; it does not report evidence about lexical-tone preservation across unseen tonal languages. The broader goal supplies a lexical-tone error requirement, but this proposed design should not be presented as having satisfied it.
How does the proposal connect to keeping source intonation and rhythm, without claiming it succeeds?

It retains explicit source-side conditioning for F0, energy, and durations while supplying target-speaker identity through separate embeddings. That arrangement is intended to support the goal of preserving the source’s intonation and rhythm during identity transfer. Whether it actually does so remains an evaluation question, not a result stated by the proposal.
Is there a risk of implying that pitch-adversarial embeddings alone protect lexical tone?

Yes. A careful description treats them as one part of the proposed separation between speaker identity and source pitch. Source F0 is also explicitly provided, and the goal concerns lexical-tone error in the converted speech itself. Describing the embeddings as a guarantee of lexical-tone preservation would overstate the proposal.
Should the earlier numerical targets be written into the architecture description?

They can be mentioned as the goal this proposal is meant to address, but they are not architectural inputs or reported outcomes. The proposal is the conditioning scheme: XLS-R content, source F0, energy, and durations, plus pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings, supplied to a zero-shot flow vocoder. Separately, the goal calls for lexical-tone error within 2 percentage points of unconverted speech and 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at 1% false acceptance using evaluators independent of training.
Does proposing those inputs settle how we would test the speaker-verification requirement?

No. The proposed conditioning describes the conversion approach, not an evaluation protocol. The goal requires independent-of-training evaluators for the speaker-verification criterion, but this proposal names neither a verifier nor a test procedure.
I’m trying to avoid accidentally presenting this as a completed experiment. What wording keeps it clearly prospective?

Say, “We propose conditioning a zero-shot flow vocoder on XLS-R content, source F0, energy, and durations, together with pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings.” You can then say that the source-side signals are intended to retain content and prosodic information while the target-speaker embeddings are intended to transfer identity. “Propose” and “intended” keep the distinction between a design and a demonstrated outcome.
Would it be accurate to say the vocoder is conditioned jointly on these signals, rather than that one signal replaces another?

Yes. The proposal lists them as conditioning inputs to the zero-shot flow vocoder. Source F0, energy, and durations remain source-side inputs; the pitch-adversarial embeddings provide target-speaker conditioning. Nothing in the proposal says that an embedding replaces the source F0 or that XLS-R content replaces the other source signals.
Then give me a compact formulation that keeps the roles of the inputs unmistakable.

Propose a zero-shot flow vocoder conditioned on XLS-R content and the source speech’s F0, energy, and durations, along with pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings. The source-side conditions are intended to retain the utterance’s content and prosodic information while the target-speaker embeddings provide identity conditioning; whether the result meets the goal’s preservation and verification requirements is not established by the proposal itself.
Can pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings transfer identity without the target reference’s F0 overwriting the source lexical tones?

That is the central open question. The proposed separation gives the vocoder source F0 explicitly and uses pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings for identity conditioning. It is intended to let the voice take on the target speaker’s identity without substituting the target reference’s pitch pattern for the source’s tonal pattern. The proposal alone does not establish that this separation works.
What exactly would count as the target-reference F0 overwriting the source?

It would mean that pitch information associated with the target reference takes precedence over the source F0 in the converted speech, changing the source’s lexical-tone distinctions. The concern is about the resulting speech, not merely whether a target-reference F0 track appears as an explicit input.
So the proposed inputs do not include target-reference F0 as a separate contour?

Correct. The proposal names source F0 as an explicit conditioning input, alongside XLS-R content, source energy, and source durations. Its target-side conditioning is the pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings. The question is whether those embeddings can convey identity without also conveying target-reference pitch in a way that interferes with source lexical tone.
Does calling an embedding pitch-adversarial mean we can assume it contains no pitch information?

No. “Pitch-adversarial” describes the intended property of the target-speaker representation; it is not proof that all pitch information is absent or that the converted speech will preserve every source tone. The identity-transfer and tone-preservation behavior remains the issue being asked about.
Why might identity transfer and lexical-tone preservation be difficult to separate conceptually?

Both concern audible properties of the converted voice, but they place different demands on it. It should sound like the target speaker while retaining the source utterance’s tone-bearing pitch behavior. The question asks whether target-speaker conditioning can supply the first without overriding the source F0 needed for the second. It does not presume that either outcome necessarily follows from the proposed inputs.
Would success mean copying the source F0 exactly at every point?

The question is framed around preventing target-reference F0 from overwriting source lexical tones, not around a specified point-by-point F0 equality test. The broader goal is to avoid altering lexical tone or prosody and to preserve source intonation and rhythm. No exact-contour matching criterion is given here.
Then what is the distinction between retaining source tones and merely making the speech recognizable as the target speaker?

They are separate outcomes. A converted utterance could be perceived or verified as the target speaker yet still alter lexical tones if target-associated pitch displaced the source tonal pattern. Conversely, preserving the source’s tones would not alone establish that target-speaker identity transferred. This question asks whether the proposed embedding can support identity transfer without that tonal trade-off.
Is the concern that the target reference itself has lexical tones?

The question does not specify the target reference’s language or utterance. Its concern is narrower: F0 associated with the target reference must not override the source F0 in a way that changes the source’s lexical tones. We need not assume anything further about the reference to state that concern.
Could I say that pitch-adversarial embeddings are designed to keep the target’s pitch contour out of the identity signal?

You can state that as the intended separation, with appropriate caution. For example: “The pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings are intended to convey identity without imposing the target reference’s F0 on the source utterance.” That expresses the rationale without asserting that the embeddings have achieved complete pitch separation.
Would the explicit source F0 input by itself settle the question?

No. Providing source F0 makes the source pitch information available to the vocoder, but it does not, by itself, establish which conditioning information governs the converted speech. The unresolved point is whether the target-speaker embeddings permit identity transfer while the output retains the source’s lexical tones.
Should I frame target-reference F0 leakage as something that definitely happens?

No. Here it is a possibility the question is meant to examine, not a reported failure. Saying that target-reference F0 *might* interfere with source lexical tones is faithful; saying that it *does* overwrite them would claim a result not provided.
And should I say that pitch adversarial training definitely prevents it?

No. The converse would also be unsupported. The question is whether pitch-adversarial target embeddings can transfer identity without target-reference F0 overwriting source lexical tones. It does not answer that question or establish a prevention guarantee.
How does this question relate to source intonation and rhythm?

Its specific focus is the risk to source lexical tones from target-reference F0 during identity transfer. Source intonation and rhythm remain part of the broader preservation goal, but this question does not separately determine whether they are preserved. It should not be treated as a complete answer to every prosody requirement.
Does answering it require assuming a particular way of extracting the target-speaker embeddings?

No extraction method is specified. The question concerns the behavior of pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings in the proposed conditioning arrangement, regardless of unspecified implementation details. Naming a particular extraction procedure would add information not present here.
What is the cleanest way to express the tension in a single sentence?

Can pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings provide enough target identity for zero-shot conversion while allowing source F0—not pitch carried over from the target reference—to govern the source utterance’s lexical tones?
Does that wording imply source F0 must determine speaker identity too?

No. It assigns different intended roles: target-speaker embeddings convey identity, while source F0 supplies the pitch information relevant to the source utterance’s tones. The question is whether those roles can coexist in the converted speech without the target reference’s F0 displacing the source tonal pattern.
If someone answers simply “yes, because the embeddings are pitch-adversarial,” what is missing?

That answer treats a design intention as evidence of an outcome. The label “pitch-adversarial” does not itself demonstrate that identity transfers, that target-reference pitch does not intrude, or that source lexical tones survive conversion. Those are precisely the points the question leaves open.
So for now this should remain a question rather than a claim of successful tone-safe identity transfer?

Yes. It asks whether the proposed target-speaker representation can transfer identity without target-reference F0 overwriting source lexical tones. Neither successful separation nor a failure to separate them is stated here.
What hypothesis should we state about the pitch-adversarial embeddings on unseen tonal languages?

The hypothesis is that pitch-adversarial embeddings will yield a ToneER increase of no more than 2 percentage points and at least 90% independent target-speaker acceptance at a 1% false-acceptance rate (FAR) on unseen tonal languages. It is a prediction about both tone preservation and identity transfer, not a report that either threshold has been reached.
Does the ToneER figure mean that converted speech must have a ToneER of 2% or less?

No. The threshold concerns the *increase* in ToneER relative to unconverted speech: converted speech should be no more than 2 percentage points higher. It does not set an absolute ToneER of 2%, and percentage points should not be read as a 2% relative increase.
Is “no more than a 2-point increase” the same as requiring the increase to be exactly 2 points?

No. It is an upper bound. An increase below 2 percentage points would satisfy that part of the hypothesis; an increase above 2 percentage points would not. The wording does not require ToneER to rise.
And the speaker figure is a minimum rather than an exact value?
Yes. The hypothesis says *at least* 90% target-speaker acceptance, measured at 1% FAR. It does not predict exactly 90%, and the 1% FAR is the stated operating condition for the acceptance figure.
What does “independent” modify in that claim?

It refers to target-speaker acceptance evaluated independently of training. The hypothesis should not be read as relying solely on a training-time acceptance measure. It does not name a particular independent evaluator or specify its procedure.
Could I shorten the claim to “90% speaker similarity”?

That would lose important specifics. The stated outcome is at least 90% *target-speaker verification acceptance* using evaluators independent of training, at 1% FAR. “Speaker similarity” does not convey that verification criterion or its false-acceptance operating point.
Is FAR related to the ToneER threshold?

No. FAR is the false-acceptance rate for target-speaker verification; its specified value is 1%. ToneER concerns lexical-tone error, with an allowed increase of no more than 2 percentage points relative to unconverted speech. The two numbers belong to different outcomes.
How does this hypothesis bear on the question of target-reference F0 overwriting source tones?

It predicts the combination that question is concerned with: target-speaker acceptance of at least 90% while the ToneER increase stays within 2 percentage points on unseen tonal languages. Those are measurable outcomes relevant to identity transfer without substantial added lexical-tone error. Stating the prediction does not establish that target-reference F0 has been kept out of the converted speech.
Why not say directly that the embeddings prevent all target-reference F0 from affecting the output?

That would be stronger than this hypothesis. It predicts bounds on ToneER increase and target-speaker acceptance, not complete absence of target-reference pitch information. Even the word “pitch-adversarial” describes the proposed embeddings; it does not turn the predicted outcomes into a guarantee about every pitch-related effect.
So the hypothesis is about the converted speech’s outcomes, not just about what information the embedding contains?

Exactly. Its two stated outcomes are a ToneER increase of at most 2 percentage points and independent target-speaker acceptance of at least 90% at 1% FAR. It does not give a separate numerical measure of pitch information within the embeddings.
Should I include the zero-shot setting when I state it?

Yes. The prediction is for unseen tonal languages in the zero-shot voice-conversion setting under discussion. Omitting that scope could make the thresholds sound like an unrestricted claim about all conversion settings.
Does “on unseen tonal languages” tell us which languages or how many?
No. It states the scope of the hypothesis without naming languages or specifying a count. The hypothesis also does not say how results would be broken down among those languages.
If I write “the embeddings achieve these thresholds,” does that sound too conclusive?

On its own, yes: “achieve” can sound like a reported result. To preserve the hypothesis status, say “We hypothesize that pitch-adversarial embeddings will yield…” and then state both thresholds and the unseen-tonal-language condition.
Would “may yield” be more accurate than “will yield”?

Either can be framed as a hypothesis, but they convey different strength. The supplied hypothesis predicts that the embeddings *yield* the stated outcomes; “we hypothesize that they will yield” expresses that prediction while making clear it remains unverified. “May yield” would make the prediction less definite than stated.
Can I say a low ToneER increase alone would establish that speaker identity transferred?

No. The hypothesis has two distinct requirements. ToneER addresses added lexical-tone error; the at-least-90% independent target-speaker acceptance at 1% FAR addresses identity transfer. Neither figure substitutes for the other.
And high target-speaker acceptance alone would not establish the tone side?

Correct. Acceptance at the specified verification operating point would address the target-speaker criterion, but it would not tell us whether the ToneER increase stayed at or below 2 percentage points. The hypothesis predicts both at once.
Does the ToneER part also prove that source intonation and rhythm are preserved?

No. ToneER addresses lexical-tone error. Preserving source intonation and rhythm remains part of the broader goal, but this hypothesis supplies no separate intonation or rhythm metric. The ToneER bound should not be presented as a complete measure of all prosody preservation.
Is the comparison to unconverted speech still relevant when stating the ToneER increase?

Yes. An “increase” needs a baseline, and the goal identifies unconverted speech as the lexical-tone-error comparison. The hypothesis is therefore that conversion adds no more than 2 percentage points to ToneER relative to unconverted speech, not that every converted utterance has the same absolute ToneER.
Should I claim the thresholds apply separately to every unseen tonal language?

The hypothesis says the outcomes are on unseen tonal languages, but it does not specify a per-language rule or an aggregation method. It is safest to retain that wording rather than add a claim about every language individually.
Does this hypothesis specify how to train the pitch-adversarial embeddings?

No. It identifies the embeddings and the outcomes hypothesized for them. It does not add a training recipe, an adversarial objective, or an evaluation procedure beyond the stated independence and 1% FAR condition for target-speaker acceptance.
Would it be accurate to call these two thresholds a predicted trade-off?

You can describe the hypothesis as predicting that both demands can be met together: limited added ToneER and high target-speaker acceptance. Calling it a measured trade-off would imply results that have not been stated, and the hypothesis does not quantify a trade-off curve between the two.
Please phrase it in one sentence that keeps the bounds, operating point, and hypothesis status clear.

We hypothesize that, on unseen tonal languages, pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings will yield a ToneER increase of no more than 2 percentage points relative to unconverted speech while achieving at least 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at 1% FAR using evaluators independent of training.
How should we plan to examine whether the pitch-adversarial target embeddings transfer identity without disrupting source lexical tones?

Train pitch-adversarial and baseline vocoders, then test them on held-out Thai and Yoruba. The planned evaluation includes ToneER, F0 errors, rhythm errors, and independent speaker verification. This is a plan for a comparison, not a report of how either vocoder performs.
Why include baseline vocoders as well as pitch-adversarial ones?

The baselines provide a comparison for the pitch-adversarial vocoders. Looking at both would help distinguish observations about the proposed approach from observations about the evaluated vocoders more generally. The plan does not specify the baselines’ architecture or exactly how they differ from the pitch-adversarial vocoders, so we should not fill in those details.
Would it be accurate to describe the baseline as the same vocoder with adversarial training switched off?

Not from this plan alone. It calls for pitch-adversarial and baseline vocoders, but does not define the baseline that narrowly. You can say they will be trained and compared without assigning the baseline an unstated design.
What role do Thai and Yoruba play in the plan?

They are the two named held-out languages for testing. The plan specifies testing on held-out Thai and Yoruba; it does not provide further details about the held-out material or how it is divided. The key point is that evaluation is planned on those languages, not that results on them are already known.
Should I say we have already tested Thai and Yoruba?
No. The node is a plan to train the vocoders and test on held-out Thai and Yoruba. Wording such as “will test” or “plan to test” keeps the status clear.
What does ToneER contribute to that test?

ToneER addresses lexical-tone error in the converted speech. It is directly relevant to the concern that transferring target-speaker identity might alter source lexical tones. The plan names ToneER as a measure, but does not specify a scoring procedure or report a ToneER value.
Why measure F0 errors as well if ToneER covers tones?

They examine related but distinct aspects of the output. ToneER concerns lexical-tone errors, while F0 errors provide a way to examine pitch behavior more directly. Including both can inform the question of tone preservation without treating an F0-error measure as identical to ToneER. The plan does not define the exact F0-error calculation.
Could a ToneER score by itself show that the target reference’s F0 was or was not carried into the output?

Not by itself. ToneER would indicate errors in lexical tone, but it would not uniquely identify where a pitch pattern came from. F0 errors add information about pitch behavior, yet the planned measures alone should not be described as proving a specific cause of any observed change.
What are the rhythm errors meant to cover?

They address timing-related preservation in the converted speech. Rhythm is part of what the source utterance is supposed to retain during identity transfer. The plan names rhythm errors as an evaluation measure without specifying how they are calculated.
So ToneER and F0 errors should not replace the rhythm evaluation?

Correct. The plan explicitly includes all three: ToneER, F0 errors, and rhythm errors. Each directs attention to a different part of the preservation question, so collapsing them into a single pitch or tone measure would leave out a stated component.
And independent speaker verification is for the other side of the question?

Yes. It addresses whether the converted speech transfers the target speaker’s identity, while ToneER, F0 errors, and rhythm errors address aspects of retaining the source utterance. The speaker verification is to be independent; the plan does not name a particular verifier.
Could we just ask listeners whether it sounds like the target speaker instead?

That would change the stated plan. The plan specifically calls for independent speaker verification. It does not rule on other possible assessments, but we should not substitute an unstated listener test for the verification measure it names.
Does “independent” mean the verifier should not be the measure used to train the vocoders?

That is the relevant distinction: speaker verification should be independent of training rather than treated as a training-time signal demonstrating success. The plan does not specify a verifier, its training data, or its detailed protocol.
How should I connect the four measures without implying that one favorable result guarantees the rest?

Describe them as complementary parts of the planned test. ToneER examines lexical-tone error; F0 and rhythm errors examine pitch and timing-related behavior; independent speaker verification examines target-speaker identity. The plan calls for considering these together, not for inferring all of them from any single measure.
If the speaker verification were favorable, would that settle whether source tones were preserved?
No. It would speak to identity transfer, not by itself to lexical-tone preservation. That is why the plan also includes ToneER and F0 errors, alongside rhythm errors for the source’s timing.
And if ToneER were favorable, could we conclude that the output sounds like the target speaker?
No. ToneER alone would not establish target-speaker identity. Independent speaker verification is the planned check for that part of the question.
Does the plan say which vocoder will perform better on Thai or Yoruba?
No. It proposes training and testing pitch-adversarial and baseline vocoders on held-out Thai and Yoruba. It makes no performance claim for either vocoder or either language.
Does it specify that the comparison must yield identical results in Thai and Yoruba?
No. Both languages are named for held-out testing, but the plan does not predict equal results or prescribe how results across them will be combined.
Could I state that the tests will isolate pitch leakage as the cause of any tone errors?

That would overstate what is specified. The comparison and measures are relevant to the question of whether target-speaker conditioning interferes with source tones. The plan does not set out a procedure that uniquely attributes any tone error to target-reference F0.
Can you state the plan in one sentence, preserving all the named components?
Train pitch-adversarial and baseline vocoders, then test them on held-out Thai and Yoruba using ToneER, F0 errors, rhythm errors, and independent speaker verification.
What should this benchmark cover?

Benchmark adversarial versus baseline embeddings on 500 held-out Thai/Yoruba utterances. Compare ToneER, F0, and timing, and measure target-speaker acceptance with an independent speaker verifier operating at 1% false acceptance rate (FAR).
